title: Student Motivation at the End of the School Year
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart opens this piece by framing two contrasting ways to finish a school year — crawling across the finish line wishing the days away, versus marching across it grateful for the year's growth — and commits to modeling the second. He then applies the Yerkes-Dodson curve (the relationship between pressure and performance) to explain why a generic end-of-year "challenge" newsletter rubbed him the wrong way: over-pressured people need play and relief, not more challenge, while under-pressured, bored people need exactly the opposite. He translates this into a differentiation move for the final weeks of school, instructing teachers to identify one bored/listless student and one anxious/over-pressured student on their roster and to speak to each in a fundamentally different register — challenge for the former, permission to rest and reframe failure for the latter. A worked script for the anxious student ("Liane") shows what this sounds like in practice, reframing the remainder of the year as a chance to grow rather than a referendum on the student's worth. Stuart closes by naming this kind of targeted, individualized language as the real heart of differentiation.
points: Stuart uses the Yerkes-Dodson curve to argue that a single end-of-year motivational message (like a generic "challenge") will land differently, and sometimes backfire, depending on whether a student is over-pressured or under-pressured.

His practical move is to identify one bored student and one anxious/failure-averse student per class and address each with a different kind of 30-60 second conversation: challenge for the bored, permission and reframing for the anxious.
The worked script for the anxious student reframes the remaining weeks as "the only way to fail was to get down on ourselves," decoupling performance anxiety from self-worth.
Stuart's definition of differentiation here is relational rather than curricular: differentiating how you approach the hearts of individual students, not the content or assignments.
quotes: We can crawl across the finish line, counting down the seconds until it's summer break because we can't wait for a rest. OR we can march across the finish line, limping a bit from the hardships of these past years, heads held high, hearts full.

When folks are on the left side of the curve, like I was, the last thing they'll respond well to is someone offering a challenge; these folks are over-pressured already, and challenge is the language of pressure.

BUT, when folks are on the right side of the curve, then what they absolutely need to experience a performance enhancement IS a challenge! They are under-pressurized and, as a result, are probably experiencing boredom and ennui.
What if we made class into a chance to grow and be with people we like — not some dark place where we're constantly failing to prove our worth?
You're not differentiating the content students are learning or the assignments in your classroom so much as you're differentiating the ways in which you approach the hearts of your young people.
